5a38c848a5f9b5bf79bb5b76739d9f6d.text: A Rotary Peace Pole featuring six different languages including Tsilhqot’in, Carrier, Metis, Secwepemc, English and French has been installed in Williams Lake. A dedication ceremony was held for a peace pole located in front of Williams Lake City Hall on Wednesday, Oct 21. Williams Lake is now home to a beacon of hope the Rotary Club of Williams Lake hopes will inspire people to come together and work towards a more peaceful world. A Rotary Peace Pole was recently installed in front of Williams Lake City Hall with a gathering and dedication ceremony held Wednesday, Oct. 21. The eight foot tall, four side pole has “May Peace be in our Communities” written in Tsilhqot’in, Carrier, Metis, Secwepemc, English and French, and also a Braille plaque. Following an opening prayer by William Lulua with Williams Lake First Nation and the singing and drumming of an honour song, Rotary Club of Williams Lake past president and current treasurer Amber Stratton said the pole is now part of a global family of more than 250,000 in over 180 countries around the world. “A peace pole is an internationally recognized symbol of the hopes and dreams of the entire human family,” Stratton said. “It stands as a quiet, visual reminder of our shared wish for one simple yet powerful vision, “May Peace Prevail on Earth.”” Stratton provided a brief overview of the origins of the peace pole that was born by Masahisa Goi following the devastation of World War II and droppings of atomic bombs. She said he came to believe that by speaking, acting and living in the spirit of the mantra “May Peace Prevail on Earth” we could radiate love, harmony and peace throughout all creation. “Peace poles are intended to inspire unity among people of all backgrounds and cultures, and to serve as silent and enduring mantras for peace,” Stratton said, adding Rotary Peace Poles reflect the global service organization’s commitment to peace building and conflict prevention while serving as an important reminder that

bcf289712d9c3f1e85770c38af12b3d1.text: Williams Lake First Nation and Thompson Rivers University signed Yerí7 me7 sucwentwécw-kt, an agreement on Tuesday, Oct. 20 to expand academic opportunities for T’exelcemc students. Williams Lake First Nation (WLFN) and Thompson Rivers University (TRU) signed an Yerí7 me7 sucwentwécw-kt, an agreement aimed at improving educational outcomes for T’exelcemc students. The new agreement was signed on Tuesday, Oct. 20, and outlines how the two parties will work together on academic programs, research and shared decisions, while acknowledging T’exelc’s inherent rights, jurisdiction, and cultural authority within its traditional territory. In an Oct. 22 release on TRU’s website, WLFN Chief Willie Sellars said, “We take great pride in building relationships and partnerships with institutions like Thompson Rivers University, operating within T’exelcemc territory and lifting up both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people across our region.” Sellars further added these partnerships create meaningful opportunities to advance reconciliation, and education is a key part of that work. He said, “By supporting learning, sharing knowledge and creating opportunities for people to better understand one another, we can help build a stronger future for everyone in our region.” The new agreement includes a joint implementation plan to put the new formalized agreement into practice. Dr. Airini, TRU president and vice-chancellor, while expressing gratitude for working together as partners with T’exelc, said, “*Yerí7 me7 sucwentwécw-kt, We will recognize one another* reflects our shared commitment to creating meaningful opportunities through education and research.” She said, “We recognize the importance of T’exelcemc knowledge, language and leadership in shaping how we work together. 3e140a3cef6fa5ff5c1ba09e11d4d83c.text: Riley Windeler holds a copy of his recently published children's book Tommy’s Race at Riverside Park in Kamloops. It has been ten years in the making for Riley Windeler who has finally released his first children’s book that he hopes empowers kids in the Cariboo and beyond. The debut author who was born and raised in Horsefly but currently resides in Kamloops has a form of short-limbed dwarfism called Hypochondroplasia. Despite his small stature of four feet and six inches Windeler hasn’t let that stand in the way, serving as inspiration for *Tommy’s Race.* He received a copy of his long awaited work that is illustrated by Nora Kelly of Montreal, Que. from Caitlin Press late last month. “It has been a whole process,” Windeler said of his long awaited book. “Now it’s here and now it’s done.” *Tommy’s Race* is based off of a race from Windeler’s childhood in the small rural community east of Williams Lake. He clearly remembers the end of his first school sports day when he was about six-years-old and his friends crossed the finish line completing the race while he was still half down the field. “That was the first real time it hit me that Ok there’s this difference here,” Windeler said. *Tommy’s Race* begins with a young character named Tommy participating in a similar such race and despite coming in last place later going to a World Dwarf Athletic event after months of training to compete on a level playing field, making friends and having the courage to win. “It’s showing that yes there are these challenges but there’s also opportunities out there between the two,” Windeler said, smiling. Windeler himself persevered while he was younger playing hockey and baseball. While he said he knows he might not have been the best player he remained passionate about the sport and enjoyed playing, being awarded the most inspirational and most dedicated player by the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Association. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson (left) and B.C. NDP leader David Eby on the campaign trail ahead of the provincial election Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. The B.C. Conservatives have maintained their lead in the polls three days ahead of the B.C. provincial election, but the B.C. NDP remain within striking distance according to the latest surveys. Recent polls from Angus Reid Institute and Mainstreet Research indicate the Conservatives are ahead of the NDP by three or six percentage points, respectively. The Angus Reid poll had a margin of error of three points, putting the Conservatives anywhere from 43 to 49 per cent support and the NDP in the range of 40 to 46 per cent support. Philippe Fournier, creator of 338Canada, launched the polling aggregator in 2017. He’s used it to track the last three B.C. elections, though he’s also closely followed earlier ones. Fournier told Black Press Thursday that B.C. elections rarely result in the kinds of blowouts that former NDP Premier John Horgan enjoyed over Andrew Wilkinson’s Liberals in 2020. He pointed out that in 2024, David Eby’s NDP won the popular vote only by about two percentage points, and won 47 seats — the exact threshold for a majority. “It would not take much for the NDP to drop a few points and then lose the election outright,” the polling analyst said. “Right now the polls pretty unanimously have the Conservatives ahead, although the margins vary from one pollster to the other,” Fournier added. Fournier said the polls suggest the NDP will need a strong push in the final days to retain office. “If the Conservatives match their polls and the NDP doesn’t over-perform, we’re looking at a Conservative government in B.C. 1cfff63b42dd7e57e7472e4b663031e9.text: On Oct. 20, 2026, 13 peace officers were welcomed into the RCMP's new Experienced Peace Officer (ExPO) program at BC RCMP headquarters in Surrey. A brand-new RCMP program to fast-track experienced peace officers into frontline police officers has begun, and the first troop of cadets will be training in Chilliwack. B.C. and Yukon RCMP held a ceremony at the BC RCMP headquarters in Surrey where they welcomed 13 peace officers on Oct. 20 into its new Experienced Peace Officer (ExPO) program. The 13 cadets have joined the RCMP from B.C., Yukon and Ontario and bring previous experience from various provincial, territorial and federal agencies, such as Corrections, Conservation, and Commercial Vehicle Safety and Enforcement (CVSE). They will now begin their RCMP careers through an accelerated cadet training program at the Pacific Region Training Centre in Chilliwack, which starts in November. They graduate in March 2027 and members will then be placed into frontline positions throughout B.C. and the Yukon. Assistant commissioner John Brewer, acting commanding officer of the BC RCMP, said it is a “significant milestone” and a moment worth celebrating. “Experienced peace officers bring with them a wealth of knowledge and practical experience that will make an impact in our organization,” Brewer said. The 3.5-month long ExPO training is nearly half the length of the standard six-month RCMP Depot training, which is only offered in Saskatchewan. The ExPO program was launched by BC and Yukon RCMP in July, and it is scheduled to expand to other provinces and territories in the coming months. RCMP said it recognizes the knowledge, skill and value experienced peace officers bring from previous work in the law enforcement community, and added that “by welcoming peace officers from a variety of backgrounds, the RCMP is strengthening its team while also creating an exciting option for experienced peace officers” to move forward with a career in policing. “The ExPO program reflects

ce0d1981110df369e51706c932da6fbb.text: The Veterans Review and Appeal Board upheld a 2019 Veterans Affairs decision to deny disability benefits to a 50-year-old RCMP officer after a severe abdominal injury required surgery. The officer, who is not named, had been on the force since 2008. While working in 2016 as a general duty officer for the Quesnel RCMP, the officer suffered severe abdominal pain and distention to the point that he could not put his duty belt back on. He began to feel a fever, chills and severe pain. His family doctor referred him to a surgeon. A CT scan showed a perforation in the large intestine and he underwent two emergency surgeries, used a colostomy bag for four months and had colostomy reversal surgery. “Currently on gradual return to work plan for work with limited hours. Possible hernia will always be a concern if/when I return to full duty,” said his submission. He was diagnosed with Perforated Diverticulosis, but Veterans Affairs Canada found it was not directly related to his work. In the July appeal decision, published in October, the board agreed that physical activity and compressive clothing or gear caused him pain an discomfort. “However, regrettably, the panel is unable to conclude that the applicant’s claimed condition of Perforated Diverticulosis arose out of, is directly related to or is aggravated by his service in the RCMP,” said the decision. **Election** **Conservatives remain ahead in polls as B.C. election day nears**](https://wltribune.com/2026/10/22/conservatives-remain-ahead-in-polls-as-b-c-election-day-nears/)

57a77d2b6ca0404caf3fcc3e79ad871e.text: Quesnel RCMP are asking for witnesses and dashcam footage following a fatal pedestrian hit-and-run near Yellow Marker earlier this month. According to an RCMP press release, the incident occurred shortly before 3 a.m. on Oct. 5, when officers were called to Highway 97 south after a report of a man sitting on the side of the road. Mounties said the man was located and taken to the hospital with what initially appeared to be minor injuries. According to police, the man later died in the hospital from injuries sustained in what was determined to be a hit-and-run incident. Following an investigation, police determined the man had been struck by a red 2023 Volvo tractor-trailer. Mounties have since located the vehicle and identified its driver. “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the victim during this distressing time,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said in the release. “What police officers are requesting is for any witnesses or anyone with dash camera footage that captures the incident to please come forward and provide their information.” Mounties said investigators are particularly seeking footage from vehicles travelling along Highway 97 south near Yellow Market between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on Oct. 5. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Quesnel RCMP non-emergency line at 250-992-9211.

5822afe96735552b2f3759df5c2f1bdb.text: ​Billie Christiansen, the founder of the Little Kitchen Company, will be featured on an upcoming episode of Dragons’ Den, a reality TV series where entrepreneurs pitch their business ideas and inventions to a panel of venture capitalists in hopes of securing financial investment and mentorship. ​Christiansen tells Black Press Media her latest creation is built around demand-driven innovation by developing original and practical products that solve frustrations that arise in the kitchen. ​“Rather than simply introducing variations of existing products, my focus is on creating genuinely innovative kitchen tools with thoughtful engineering, premium materials and distinctive designs. That commitment to innovation has resulted in 13 patents worldwide: one granted and 12 pending,” said Christiansen. ​Her latest invention, called the Twist, is a stainless steel chicken shredder and, according to her, is the only one in the world. ​Christiansen can’t give away what happens on the show, but she said it was a nerve-racking experience. ​The local entrepreneur uses software to identify high consumer demand for products that don’t exist. ​“From there, I essentially reverse-engineer the product development process, design it, create prototypes, patent it, manufacture it and bring it to market,” she explained. ​Christiansen claims her first invention, a stainless steel meat chopper, was No. 1 on Amazon New Releases for 90 straight days. ​Those who love cooking and puttering around the kitchen can catch Christiansen on Dragons’ Den when episode nine of season 21 airs on Thursday, Nov. 12, on CBC. **Election** **Conservatives remain ahead in polls as B.C. election day nears**](https://wltribune.com/2026/10/22/conservatives-remain-ahead-in-polls-as-b-c-election-day-nears/)

e53bbe063a7ba2ff9e9a592a639bf7cf.text: Berta, a five-year-old Maremma livestock guardian dog, was discovered dead in a baited snare near her home west of Williams Lake. “If I would have known the dangers in my backyard, maybe she would have been able to be saved,” is the thought that keeps coming back to Victoria Savile of Williams Lake as she calls for change after her family’s beloved dog, Berta, was killed in a baited snare not far from their home. Savile has recently joined The Fur-Bearers, a Canadian wildlife protection charity dedicated to protecting fur-bearing animals through conservation, advocacy, research and education. She’s also working with Nicole Trigg whose dog, Moon, was killed by a baited trap off a public service road in the East Kootenays earlier this year. Berta died after becoming entangled in the trap Savile said was set not far from their property in the Pablo Creek area west of Williams Lake, in an area she has ridden her horses, hiked and hunted for the past eight years. Savile had never seen a snare, bait or been told a trapping line was present until Berta’s body was discovered on Sunday, Oct. 18 by a neighbour out quadding. In shock and overcome with emotion that morning, Savile called the RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) line and in less than an hour conservation officers arrived to remove the trap from Berta, who had failed to return home earlier this month. She said officers helped load Berta’s body into her and her family’s truck, which they brought back home to bury in their backyard. Berta was a five-year-old Maremma livestock guardian dog adopted in Alberta who Savile described as a great protector in keeping predators away and everyone safe, including their neighbour’s sheep and goats. Her family loved calling her ‘Dirty Bert’ due to the fact her pure white coat was always stained by dirt that no one knew where from. “She was an absolute sweetheart and her life was taken from us,” Savile said. fbe7446fb20855b6af3b469b8a555cdf.text: Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor is presented with the first poppy this year by Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 First Vice President Al Tranq. The Royal Canadian Legion's National Poppy Campaign runs from Oct. 24 to Nov. 11. Poppies will be available in Williams Lake starting Friday, Oct. 23 as the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 distributes poppy boxes to local businesses in advance of Remembrance Day. The first poppy was presented earlier this week to Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor by Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 First Vice President Al Tranq at the cenotaph located outside city hall where flags were flying at half-mast in recognition of the tragic deaths at the Canadian Forces Base (CFB) in Wainwright. “Each year, Canadians step up with amazing support for the National Poppy Campaign,” stated Royal Canadian Legion Dominion President Sharon McKeown in a news release. “Their generosity and caring are what allow us to host a range of programs and support initiatives for our Veterans and their families across the country.” Poppies will be available right up until Nov. 11 where in Williams Lake there will be an indoor ceremony at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex starting 10 a.m. in the Gibraltar Room. Doors open at 9 a.m. The Colour Party and those marching will then head over to the cenotaph outside city hall for a moment of silence and a wreath-laying ceremony. They’ll then march to the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 located at 385 Barnard St. to lay a wreath after which everyone is invited into the branch for food and camaraderie. A wreath or cross for the cenotaph display can still be rented by emailing poppy139@gmail.com or calling 250-305-7999.

The Vancouver-Quilchena riding, deep within a leafy-green, wealthy Vancouver neighbourhood, has long been a bastion of B.C.’s right wing. Former B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is still explaining why he dissolved the legislature and called the snap vote when his party still had two years left on its mandate. “People are very surprised and frustrated by the election call,” he told reporters in Surrey on Friday. “I should have done a better job of letting them know how stalled out the legislature was.” His opponents have capitalized, with leaders of both the Conservative and Green parties calling it a “cynical” power grab. Eby called it his “biggest regret” of the campaign that he didn’t do a better job of filling voters in and convincing them it is needed for his party to govern effectively. Since the 2024 election, Eby’s party has shuffled along with a one-vote majority and often struggled to muster the votes to pass difficult legislation, such as amendments to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. In a sit-down interview on his campaign bus as he veered between key Lower Mainland ridings on the final day before election day, he explained the difficulties he says his government faced. “Even things as simple as allowing pets in rentals had to be sacrificed to be able to get other pieces through,” he said, referring to a 2024 election promise to mandate landlords allow pets in purpose-built rental buildings. 59f61017c339b9e4fa7288bea8865319.text: NDP leader David Eby (right) visited downtown Langley City with local candidates Holly Isaac (left) and Andrew Mercier (centre). NDP leader David Eby (right) visited downtown Langley City with local candidates Holly Isaac (left) and Andrew Mercier (centre). NDP leader David Eby said the 300-bed long-term care facility his government promised Langley before the last election would be built if he’s re-elected. Eby met with Langley-Willowbrook NPD candidate Andrew Mercier and Langley-Walnut Grove’s hopeful Holly Isaac on Friday, Oct. 23, in Langley City, visiting several local stores and chatting with people on the street in the final hours before the provincial election. Asked about the promised local facility, which was to be built on the grounds of Langley Memorial Hospital, Eby said there had been challenges in bringing down the per-bed cost of that planned facility and a number of others. The province was working to drive down the cost via standardization, he said. “Shovels will be in the ground on this and seven other long-term care facilities,” Eby said. He also acknowledged the need for more hospital services in the fast growing South of the Fraser region. “We need more health-care professionals and health-care services,” Eby said, arguing that the NDP’s plan would be fully funded, while alleging that the B.C. Conservatives would cut health services. The Conservatives have promised to protect health-care funding, recruit more doctors and nurses, and cut wait times. On another local issue, Mercier said that the NDP is promising a second Urgent Primary Care facility for Langley. The first local UPC opened in May 2024. They’re intended to take some pressure off overburdened hospital emergency rooms. Eby said that the funding for a new UPC could also be applied to a community health centre, a model in which towns and cities can have their own building with similar services and some municipal control. A playful rivalry is heating up between the University of Victoria (UVic) and the star of the hit hockey romance TV series that has taken the world by storm. While promoting new drama series Yaga, filmed in and around Victoria, Heated Rivalry actor Hudson Williams offered a less-than-favourable review of B.C.’s capital when asked to name the city’s “hot spots.” “A lot of hot spots of, like, old people on their little scooters, people retiring,” he told Etalk. “Like, it’s Victoria. Hotspots for, like, what? Like retirement homes and fricking bingo, like that’s it. It’s not the first time the actor has taken a playful jab at Victoria’s reputation. During a break from filming in March, the 25-year-old actor was caught on camera at a Paris fashion show delivering another less-than-flattering take on Victoria. “I was filming a show, and it’s very stabilizing,” he said. “It’s like 30 minutes away from Vancouver, dead as f\*\*\*, old people.” However, days later when filming wrapped, Williams softened his stance, sharing a more affectionate farewell to the city on social media. “That’s it for me on Yaga Victoria: Old people + Dead asf + Nature = Feels like home/heart gets full,” he wrote. While Williams’ words appear to be tongue-in-cheek, UVic isn’t letting the jabs go unanswered. The university has fired back at the actor with a playful social media post that pokes fun at his review while highlighting some of Greater Victoria’s attractions. 092f76289e140047d724462021b890f7.text: After the posted asphalt resurfacing project was actually seal coating, upset residents are frustrated with the large, loose rocks and jagged surface that are damaging vehicles. Jeff Seabrook shows the size of the rocks that now cover Chase-Falkland Road as a result of resurfacing work recently completed by the province. “This new road is supposed to be an upgrade, and it’s the exact opposite.” Jeff Seabrook, a resident of Chase-Falkland Road that was supposed to have asphalt resurfacing, said they’re literally getting dinged by the “bait and switch” project, and their vehicles are paying the price. According to a June 9 media release from the Ministry of Transportation and Transit (MoTT), more than $136 million was invested this year to resurface interior highways and local roads to ensure “drivers continue to have a safe and comfortable driving experience.” The project included 28.7 kilometres of Chase-Falkland. Seabook said the road’s new surface, rather than asphalt, was a seal coating that is just “loose rocks with oil mixed into and pressed down with a roller.” The result, he added, is neither “safe” nor “comfortable.” “I drive it every day… and before it was fine, there was a couple potholes, but your car wasn’t getting damaged,” Seabrook said. “But this new road is supposed to be an upgrade, and it’s the exact opposite, and the fact that they’re promoting that it’s resurfaced asphalt is a joke.” Seabrook said said he and others thought the seal coating was part of the prep work for the asphalt, but the “completed” tag on a B.C. government sign placed along the road suggests the job is done. “When you do a bad job in the private sector, you get fired. There’s consequences,” Seabrook pointed out. “Never mind the fraud part of it. 6f6f5a70220bfb22658046536855d2f2.text: Quesnel RCMP are asking for witnesses and dashcam footage following a fatal pedestrian hit-and-run near Yellow Marker earlier this month. According to an RCMP press release, the incident occurred shortly before 3 a.m. on Oct. 5, when officers were called to Highway 97 south after a report of a man sitting on the side of the road. Mounties said the man was located and taken to the hospital with what initially appeared to be minor injuries. According to police, the man later died in the hospital from injuries sustained in what was determined to be a hit-and-run incident. Following an investigation, police determined the man had been struck by a red 2023 Volvo tractor-trailer. Mounties have since located the vehicle and identified its driver. “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the victim during this distressing time,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said in the release. “What police officers are requesting is for any witnesses or anyone with dash camera footage that captures the incident to please come forward and provide their information.” Mounties said investigators are particularly seeking footage from vehicles travelling along Highway 97 south near Yellow Market between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on Oct. 5. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson at a rally in Surrey on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Lorne Doerkson has been sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo-Chilcotin, this time as premier of the entire province. Based on preliminary polls Doerkson, the incumbent MLA for the Conservative Party of B.C., has won 76.9 per cent of the vote as of 10:30 p.m., with 75 of 89 ballot boxes counted. His rivals, Kathryn Askew of the BC NDP, secured roughly 17.1 per cent of the vote, while Douglas Gook of the Green Party of B.C. brought home six per cent of the vote. As of Saturday, Oct. 24 at 9 p.m., the Conservative Party of B.C. is on track to form a majority government. This means that, if Doerkson’s interim-leader status is formalized, he will be B.C.’s next premier. Projections currently predict a 64-seat majority government for the Conservatives, with the NDP set to form the opposition with 27 seats. Speaking to a crowd of supporters Saturday night in Victoria, Doerkson was visibly excited and emotional. In his speech, he praised the volunteers who made this victory possible, both provincially and here in the Cariboo-Chilcotin. “To our volunteers, you knocked on doors, rain and shine, you did so much incredible work. You put up signs, you made the calls, none of this would have been possible without your hard work,” Doerkson said. “To everyone who voted tonight, including those who voted for someone else, thank you so very much. “I also want to thank my team at home, because they have done an unbelievable job. I will say this, Cariboo-Chilcotin is amazing!” During his speech, Doerkson mentioned the Cariboo several times when outlining his vision for B.C.’s future. 1a2abfe921b2de6235b0b7bf6f6b14ac.text: Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win | Williams Lake Tribune Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win Lorne Doerkson takes the stage as the B.C. Conservatives are the projected 2026 election winners by majority. Lorne Doerkson is poised to become British Columbia’s next premier after leading the Conservative Party to a projected majority government Saturday, Oct. 24, barely five weeks after taking over a party struggling with internal divisions. A projected Conservative majority was solidified shortly after 9 p.m., prompting loud cheers and sustained applause from supporters gathered at the party’s election-night headquarters at Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver. An estimated 500 to 600 people attended the gathering, where supporters repeatedly erupted in applause as election results appeared on screens throughout the evening. Doerkson, 58, assumed the party’s interim leadership Sept. 20 following Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation. Two days later, NDP Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election, sending British Columbians to the polls two years ahead of schedule. Doerkson is also being sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo Chilcotin. The Conservatives established leads across much of the province on Saturday, including several Metro Vancouver ridings previously held by the NDP. Doerkson was first elected to the legislature in 2020 as a BC Liberal, representing Cariboo-Chilcotin, and joined the Conservatives in 2024. Before entering provincial politics, he worked as a community newspaper publisher. His appointment as interim leader followed months of Conservative infighting, caucus departures and changes in party leadership. Following his appointment, several MLAs who had left or been expelled returned to the Conservative caucus. 150448b73a0f1e2ebf11526ab858bb91.text: B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream has a new MLA, as the BC Conservatives’ Pavneet Singh has been elected. Singh beat out BC NDP candidate Binny Boparai, Green candidate Carter Mochinski and OneBC candidate Alexandra Wright to win the riding. In a brief interview with media, Singh thanked volunteers and supporters. Media, including Black Press, were barred by the Conservative campaign managers on scene from listening to Singh’s victory speech at the Fairfield Inn on Powick Road on election night on Oct. 24. Singh told media, “Today is not the time for media interviews, today is for the volunteers, family and friends who supported us.” Singh said he would be available for interview at a later date. With one ballot box left to be counted, Singh has 47.44 per cent of the vote (10,453 votes).

With a Conservative Party of BC majority government forecast, and with Conservative candidate Megan Knight projected to win the riding of Surrey South, CentreBC leader and Surrey South candidate Elenore Sturko was a little emotional as she spoke to her team at CentreBC headquarters Saturday night. The CentreBC office was filed with positive energy throughout election night, despite the party not being projected to win any seats in the provincial legislature. “I’m a bit emotional as I deliver this speech tonight, but please know it’s not because I’m sad. It’s because I’ve so enjoyed serving my community and the gravity of knowing how many of you supported me during these last four years of elected service, and now that that is changing, it’s heavy,” Sturko told her supporters, other CenterBC candidates, and volunteers after former NDP premier David Eby conceded the majority Conservative win. “Tonight the results may not be what we hoped for. We may not have won a seat in the legislature and I know it’s disappointing because we did work hard. We believed in what we were building and we wanted the opportunity to put our ideas into action. But I want you to remember something,” Sturko continued. “The value of what we have accomplished cannot be measured by the number of seats that we’ve won tonight. Just weeks ago Center BC was a party with potential but limited resources, a small team, and a long work ahead of us. Together we built something very special. We recruited candidates across British Columbia. We brought new voices into public life, developed great platforms focused on practical solutions, and took our message directly to the people,” she said. NDP leader, concedes to Conservatives Lorne Doerkson the B.C. Conservative interim leader has taken the projected win for the party to form a majority government. B.C. provincial party leaders from left: B.C. Greens Leader Emily Lowan, CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, B.C. Conservatives Leader Lorne Doerkson, B.C. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has pledged to get British Columbia’s economy back on track after leading the Conservatives to a projected majority government Saturday evening. “B.C. is definitely blue,” Doerkson told supporters during his victory speech at the party’s Vancouver election-night gathering. He promised to encourage investment, increase liquefied natural gas production and deliver on his campaign commitment not to introduce new taxes. Doerkson, who took over the party’s interim leadership just five weeks ago, thanked outgoing Premier David Eby for his years of public service and congratulated Green Party Leader Emily Lowan on her election victory. Although the Conservatives have secured a projected majority government, several individual ridings are still too close to call. Elections BC’s 10:31 p.m. results show the Conservatives leading the NDP by just 21 votes in Cowichan Valley and 89 votes in Kelowna Centre. In Burnaby South-Metrotown, the NDP holds a 39-vote advantage, with only one ballot box outstanding in the initial count. Provincewide, Conservatives lead in 63 ridings, compared with 28 for the NDP and two for the Greens. Just over 92 per cent of ballot boxes have reported, although outstanding ballots and the final count could change the outcome of close constituency races. 01a11f2c61e647ff958490237e85b77c.text: B.C. Votes 2026: Conservative Kevin Acton elected as Vernon-Lumby MLA | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. Votes 2026: Conservative Kevin Acton elected as Vernon-Lumby MLA B.C. Conservative Kevin Acton gives his victory speech on provincial election night Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. B.C. Conservative candidate Kevin Acton responds to results coming in at his election party at Okanagan Spirits Craft Distillery Saturday night, Oct. 24, 2026. Kevin Acton is the B.C. Conservative candidate for Vernon-Lumby in the Oct. 24, 2026 provincial election. Kevin Acton has been elected as Vernon-Lumby’s MLA in Saturday’s provincial snap election. The B.C. Conservative candidate has secured his first term in the B.C. Legislature, while the Conservatives have won a projected majority government. Acton celebrated the victory with friends, family and supporters at Okanagan Spirits Craft Distillery in Vernon. “I’m pretty excited, as anybody would be. It’s a massive effort that was put out by myself and my team. I don’t think anybody on my team has slept for a month, so it feels pretty good,” Acton said in a room full of boisterous supporters. He becomes his home area’s MLA for the first time, having served as Lumby’s mayor since 2009. Acton attributed his election win to the amount of work he and his team put in. “I’ve been the mayor for 17 years. People know me in the community as the chair of the regional district and the chair of the hospital district. They know I’ve put the work in,” Acton said. “And I think they’re just looking for change. I was more nervous about making sure that I do a really good job for the people than I was about winning. I really think that this community is very special and I’m hoping to be able to really make a difference here.” Acton, an entrepreneur and registered massage therapist who has lived in the riding since 1991, was voted in as Lumby’s mayor for a sixth time in last week’s local government elections. 1b4ca04c8bd0ed76c493ca7411c36478.text: Polls now closed in B.C. election, counting underway | Williams Lake Tribune A Voting Place sign outside AJ McLellan Elementary School in Surrey on Oct. 16, 2026. Polls have closed across B.C., and counting has started except in Grassy Plains, on the Southside of Francois Lake in the Nechako Lakes riding of Northwest B.C., where the polling station will remain open until 10 p.m. Elections B.C. confirmed that voters on the Southside would have the extra two hours tonight after the polls opened late this morning, after 10 a.m. Today, Oct. 24, is the final day to vote in the provincial election. British Columbians are heading to the polls to vote for MLAs in 93 ridings across the province. Polls opened at 8 a.m. and will close at 8 p.m., local time. A live blog will be updated throughout the evening with coverage from party headquarters. NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22 after about a week of speculation as the B.C. Conservative Party dissolved into chaos, and Kerry-Lynne Findlay quit as party leader. Two days before the election call, Lorne Doerkson was named interim Conservative leader, unifying the party and bringing more than a dozen MLAs who had quit under Findlay back into the fold before the election was called. Five parties with incumbent MLAs are hoping to expand their seat count: the NDP, the Conservative Party, the Green Party, CentreBC and OneBC. There are also a handful of smaller parties and Independents. For a list of final voting day locations across the province, click here.

As of Oct. 24, 2026 the nearly 1,300 USW Local 7619 workers at the site are on strike. The 1,277 members of United Steelworkers (USW) Local 7619 at Teck Highland Valley Copper (HVC) near Kamloops went on strike as of Saturday (Oct. 24). The collective agreement between USW Local 7619 and HVC expired on Sept. 30. Negotiations regarding terms and conditions for a new collective agreement began on June 9, with meetings continuing throughout July, August, and September. On Oct. 8, the union broke off talks with HVC to seek a strike mandate, and union members took part in a two-day strike vote on Oct. 16 and 17. According to the bargaining committee, 944 members voted in what was described as the strongest strike vote in the history of the local. The final tally showed that 100 per cent of those who voted were in favour of serving 72-hour strike notice, which was issued at 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 20 after HVC provided a monetary counter and removed one concession, but left other concession requests in place. An update on Oct. 21 noted that HVC had reached out to continue bargaining. However, talks between USW and HVC on Oct. 21 and 22 failed to result in a new collective agreement. On Saturday, strike captains were organizing picket lines at the main gate of Highland Valley Copper on Highway 97C between Ashcroft and Logan Lake, where union members were being directed to go to. Drivers are advised to exercise caution through the area. In addition to proposed concessions from HVC, negotiations have centred around wages, pensions, staff shortages, and retention. Incumbent Sheldon Clare is projected to be re-elected in Prince George-North Cariboo. Clare, representing the BC Conservative Party, faced BC NDP candidate Denice Bardua and BC Green Party candidate Randy Thompson in the 2026 provincial election. As of 9 p.m. on Oct. 24, 10 out of 71 polls have been reported so far. Clare has secured 5,148 votes or 69.3 per cent of the total. Bardua has secured 1,613 votes, or 21.7 per cent, and Thompson secured 666 votes or nine per cent. Clare was first elected in 2024, when he secured 11,430 votes, or 56.82 per cent of the total. Back in 2024, independent candidate Coralee Oakes finished second in that election with 21.84 per cent of the vote, while Bardua received 17.03 per cent and Thompson garnered just over four per cent. Both Bardua and Thompson returned to contest the riding in 2026, challenging Clare for the seat. In an interview with the _Observer,_ Clare said the result did not come as a surprise. “I’ve been in contact with lots of people. Conservative majority government. When inquired about the projection, Clare called it “terrific.” “I think that with majority comes great responsibility. You can’t be a bully government.
